newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan securities firm Yamaichi to sue over reports.
newsitem.headline: Japan securities firm Yamaichi to sue over reports.

text.p: Leading brokerage Yamaichi Securities Co on Monday denied media reports about its business dealings and said it would file libel suits against a Japanese newspaper and a business magazine.

A spokesman for Yamaichi, Japan's fourth-biggest brokerage, said a report in Monday's edition of mass-circulation daily Sankei Shimbun on the brokerage's past dealings with steel wholesaler Hanwa Co Ltd was "totally groundless".
Hanwa said there had been no illegality in transactions between it and Yamaichi. A spokesman for the Sankei Shimbun was not immediately available to comment.

Separately, Yamaichi said on Monday it would also file a suit against publisher Toyo Keizai Inc over an article in its weekly business magazine. A spokesman for Toyo Keizai declined to comment, saying it had heard nothing from Yamaichi about the action.

On the Tokyo stock market on Monday, the media reports helped push down Yamaichi's shares by eight yen by midday, traders said. But by the close of trade the share price was up one yen at 355 yen. Turnover was 3.64 million shares.

Last week, Yamaichi chairman Tsugio Yukihira told a news conference that the company had no illegal "tobashi" deals, in which brokers seek to hide a client's investment losses by transferring them to another client's account.
He was responding to a question about Japanese media reports in the past month that Yamaichi had carried out such deals.

Asked about media claims that Yamaichi had conducted tobashi deals worth 400 billion yen ($3.20 billion), Yukihira said: "I would like to decline to comment...but because this matter relates to confidence in the industry, I must say that we don't have any such deals at all."

Japan's securities industry, already hurt by falling commissions due to a stagnant Tokyo stock market, suffered a setback last month when industry leader Nomura Securities Co Ltd said two of its directors were involved in suspected illegal deals in which substantial sums of Nomura money were moved to the account of a corporate customer who media reports have said is linked to a former "sokaiya" racketeer.
Sokaiya extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt shareholders' meetings. The scandal led Nomura's president to resign to take management responsibility. ($1=125 yen)
